edits.before: Lin Xiangru came back from the meeting at Mianchi and was made shangqing, the highest ministerial rank, placed above Lian Po. Lian Po was Zhao's finest general: he had beaten Qi, taken Yangjin and won a name for courage among the states. His reaction was blunt. Lin Xiangru had earned his place with nothing but his tongue; why should he sit above me? He announced that the next time they met he would humiliate the man. What makes the episode hard is that, by Lian Po's own account, he had great merit from storming cities and fighting in the field, while Lin Xiangru's credit was entered under words. Now both held the top rank at court: one meant to humiliate, the other hid.

edits.before: 到了秦廷，秦王在章台接见相如，接过璧大喜，传给身边的美人和侍从看，左右都高呼万岁。相如看出秦王无意偿城，上前说璧有小毛病要指给秦王看，拿到璧便退立倚柱，怒发上冲冠，当面斥责秦王，放话「臣頭今與璧倶碎於柱矣」；直到此时才「持其璧睨柱，欲以撃柱」。秦王怕他砸碎，连忙道歉，召来管图籍的官员，指着地图说从这里过去的十五座城给赵。相如判断这不过是做样子，城根本拿不到，于是说和氏璧是天下共传之宝，赵王送来前斋戒五日，秦王也该斋戒五日，设九宾于廷，他才敢献璧。秦王答应了，把他安置在广成传舍。相如断定秦王即便斋戒也一定违约，就让随从穿上粗布衣，把璧揣在怀里，从小路逃走，送回赵国。等再次上廷，他把话摊开：秦自缪公以来二十多位国君，没有一位说话算数；璧已送回赵国，「臣知欺大王之罪當誅，臣請就湯鑊」。秦王与群臣相视而嘻，左右有人要把他拉下去，秦王最终说，杀了相如也得不到璧，反而断了秦赵之好，不如以礼相待送他回去，「卒廷見相如，畢禮而歸之」。

edits.before: At the Qin court the king received Lin Xiangru in the Zhang Terrace, was delighted with the jade, and passed it around to his ladies and attendants, who all cried long life to him. Lin Xiangru saw he had no intention of paying. He said the gem had a small flaw he would point out, took it back and stood against a pillar, his hair bristling with anger, and denounced the king, warning that he would dash his own head and the jade together against the pillar. Only then did he stand holding the jade with his eyes on the pillar, ready to bring it down. The alarmed king apologised, sent for the official in charge of maps and pointed out fifteen cities for Zhao. Lin Xiangru judged this mere show. The Heshi jade was a treasure the whole world talked of, he said; the king of Zhao had fasted five days before sending it, and the king of Qin should fast five days and hold the nine-fold ceremony at court before he would dare present it. The king agreed and lodged him at the Guangcheng hostel. Sure that the king would break his word even after fasting, Lin Xiangru had a follower put on coarse clothes, hide the jade in his robe and take it home to Zhao by back roads. At the next audience he laid it out: in more than twenty reigns since Duke Mu, Qin had never kept a firm agreement; the jade was already back in Zhao; "I know that deceiving Your Majesty is a crime deserving death, and I ask to go to the cauldron." The king and his ministers looked at one another and laughed wryly. Some attendants moved to drag him out, but the king reasoned that killing him would not bring back the jade and would end good relations with Zhao. In the end he received Lin Xiangru at court with full ceremony and sent him home.

edits.before: Lin Xiangru's yielding was not simple endurance either. The reason he gave his retainers was not that Lian Po was beneath notice, but a judgment about the whole board: the reason mighty Qin has not dared to send its armies against Zhao is only that the two of us are still here. edits.before: Within the same biography the gesture of admitting fault appears twice. Lin Xiangru's advice to Miao Xian was to strip and lie on the block to ask pardon; when Lian Po came to the gate, he came stripped to the waist with thorns on his back. Both are postures of baring the body and handing it over. One cannot say that Lian Po knew of the earlier case or was influenced by it; the parallel is the author's observation, not something the text states. Advising the king of Zhao before the mission, Lin Xiangru used a different grammar: first settle where the wrong will lie, with Zhao or with Qin, arrange for it to fall on the other side, and only then decide how far to give. The Grand Historian's verdict: he stepped back and yielded to Lian Po, and his name came to weigh as much as Mount Tai.
edits.after: Within the same biography the gesture of admitting fault appears twice. Lin Xiangru's advice to Miao Xian was to strip and lie on the block to ask pardon; when Lian Po came to the gate, he came stripped to the waist with thorns on his back. Both are postures of baring the body and handing it over. One cannot say that Lian Po knew of the earlier case or was influenced by it; the parallel is the author's observation, not something the text states. The weighing of options recorded in the Shiji uses a different grammar: first settle where the wrong will lie, with Zhao or with Qin, and arrange for it to fall on the other side. The Grand Historian's verdict: he stepped back and yielded to Lian Po, and his name came to weigh as much as Mount Tai.
